teaching.causalExplanation: Start with the apples. Most weigh close to a hundred and seventy-five grams, and there are about as many a bit lighter as a bit heavier. Fold the histogram down the middle, at a hundred and seventy-five, and the two halves land on each other. That's a symmetric distribution. The left side is a mirror image of the right. Each side thins out into a tail, the thin end on each side, and here the two tails match. That makes sense for apples. They grow towards a typical size, and small differences either way are equally likely. Lots of things made or grown to one size look like this, like the amount of drink a machine pours into each bottle. Now screen time. Here the two sides don't match. Most students sit between two and four hours, and then the bars thin out slowly to the right, all the way to seven and a half hours. One tail is longer than the other, so the distribution is skewed. The long tail points towards the bigger numbers, the positive end, so it's positively skewed. Screen time can't go below nought, but a few students use their phone for hours, and they stretch the tail out. Sleep is the other way round. Most students slept six and a half to eight and a half hours. Below that the values thin out, six, then five and a half, then one night of just three. That tail points left, towards the smaller numbers, so sleep is negatively skewed. Both shapes have just one peak. It's only the tails that differ. Notice the sleep peak is on the right. People often name the skew by the peak, and get it backwards. Name it by the tail. Here's why the peak and the tail sit on opposite sides. This histogram starts symmetric. Drag its tail out to the right. A few values stretch far out on that side, but the many ordinary values stay bunched where they were. Now it's positively skewed, with the peak on the left of the long tail. Drag the tail out to the left instead, and the peak sits on its right. Negatively skewed. The tail is only where the few far values sit. The peak is where most of the data sit, so it ends up on the other side from the tail. So always look for the long, thin side first, and name the shape after it.

scenes.teachingReason: Shape is also about peaks. A peak is a value, or a class, that's more common than its neighbours. Screen time, sleep and apples each have one peak, so they're unimodal. Now a food truck's customers through the day. There's a rush at lunch, a dip in the afternoon, and another rush at dinner. Two peaks with a dip between, so it's bimodal. Two peaks often mean two groups mixed together, here lunch customers and dinner customers. If you see two peaks, ask what the two groups might be. A café that's busy at breakfast, lunch and after school has three peaks. More than two is multimodal. And sometimes there's no peak at all. Roll a fair die six hundred times, and each face comes up about a hundred times. A flat shape like that, where every value is about equally common, is uniform.

scenes.teachingReason: In an exam, describe a distribution in one or two sentences. Give the number of peaks, the shape, where most values are, and anything unusual, then a reason in context if you're asked. Use the units from the axis, minutes or hours. Screen time is unimodal and positively skewed. Most students used between a hundred and twenty and two hundred and forty minutes, and a few went up to four hundred and fifty-five. Sleep is unimodal and negatively skewed. Most slept six and a half to eight and a half hours, and one slept only three. Symmetric and uniform are shapes too, so use them when they fit. A shape on its own isn't a description. A shape with a reason is.
